The full passage from Foochow to the Lizard lasted 89 days, with the ship arriving on 18 September. **Record of the Cape Verde Point Lighthouse Text**

The text describes the lighthouse at Cape Verde Point, beginning with its establishment and continuing through its operational details, safety additions, and staffing history.

The lighthouse was commissioned on 3 March 1901 and was first lit by its keeper, Augusto Ferreira. Ferreira remained in charge of the light for eleven consecutive years. The tower itself rises to a height of 34 metres. Its light is produced by a dioptric apparatus of the second order, which displays two white flashes every fifteen seconds. This light can be seen from a distance of 18 nautical miles.

In terms of operation, the station burns kerosene as its fuel, consuming it at a rate of 460 litres per month. The kerosene is kept in a store that was built into the head keeper's cottage.

A fog signal was added to the station in 1904, producing two blasts per minute. This addition came about as a direct consequence of a maritime disaster: the wreck of the barque Santa Ana. The Santa Ana had struck the reef beneath the point on 9 July 1903, and seven hands were lost in the wreck.

Regarding the surrounding geography and communications, the point lies 6 kilometres north of the fishing port of Praia Seca. A telephone line connecting the station to that port was completed in 1907.

The text concludes with a change of staffing: Ferreira was succeeded in 1912 by his assistant, Joao Braz. Braz had joined the lighthouse service in 1898, meaning he had been in the service for some fourteen years before taking over the position.

This text is the log of the whaler Diana of Hull, kept by the ship's surgeon, Dr. Charles Edward Smith, during the Davis Strait fishery of 1866. The Diana was a brig-rigged steam whaler of 350 tons register, commanded by Captain John Gravill. She left Hull on 12 February with a crew of 49 hands. Of these, 8 were green hands — inexperienced men — shipped at a wage of two pounds ten shillings per month, while the seasoned men drew three pounds five shillings.

The ship crossed the Arctic Circle on 3 March, in longitude 22 degrees west, and made the ice edge off Disko on 19 March. The first whale was struck on 2 April off the Women's Islands and yielded 12 tons of oil and 9 hundredweight of bone. A second whale, taken on 17 April, yielded 15 tons. By the end of May, the catch stood at four whales and 1,400 seals.

On 11 June, the ship was nipped in the ice in Melville Bay and lost her rudder. The carpenter fashioned a temporary rudder from spare spars within three days. The vessel was then beset and drifted with the pack ice for 61 days. During this drift, the surgeon recorded the first case of scurvy on 8 July, and by the middle of August, 22 men were on the sick list. The ship's supply of lime juice had run out, so when the ship touched land on 21 August, the crew ate sorrel gathered on the Greenland coast. Three men died in the last week of August and were buried on shore.

The Diana worked free of the ice on 25 September and reached Hull on 11 October with 41 tons of oil and 3 tons of bone. The voyage was a paying one only because of the seal catch. The owners, Samuel and Charles Gourlay, declared the gross earnings at 3,860 pounds and paid each seasoned hand 19 pounds twelve shillings for the voyage.

This text is a field dispatch relating to the survey of the Bengal Nagpur railway extension. It was written at Chanda on 29 November 1889 by Mr. Reginald Shaw, the assistant engineer, and addressed to the chief engineer at Calcutta.

The dispatch reports that the survey party, which numbered 34 persons in total, including 12 chainmen and 6 sappers of the Madras Sappers, had completed the location survey of the 92-mile section running from Nagbhid to Chanda. This work was finished on 22 November, after fourteen weeks spent in the field.

As located, the line follows the Wyne Ganga valley for 41 miles, crosses that river by means of a bridge of seven spans, each 150 feet long, at Karanja, and then takes the northern flank of the hills.

Shaw estimates the earthwork for the whole section at 480,000 cubic yards, of which 62,000 cubic yards consist of rock excavation in the eleven miles beyond Ballarshah. For the crossing of the river at Karanja, three different alignments were examined. The line that was adopted is 1.7 miles longer than the southern route, but it avoids 90,000 cubic yards of rock excavation and two well sinkings.

The country between Ballarshah and Chanda is reported to be healthy, with the exception of the months of July and August, when fever caused the deaths of four chainmen during the season.

The party's expenses to date amounted to 19,400 rupees, set against a sanctioned grant of 30,000 rupees. In light of this, Shaw makes three requests: an additional 8,000 rupees to cover the next season; a theodolite to replace the one that was damaged at the Wyne Ganga crossing on 3 September; and the loan of a second survey elephant from the Chanda division, since the party's own elephant had gone lame after the monsoon.

Shaw closes the dispatch by noting that the levelling of the first 40 miles has been checked twice, and that the two checks agree with each other within 0.15 feet.

The text is a record of a British consular report concerning the wool trade of the La Plata region. The report was prepared in Buenos Aires by Her Majesty's Consul, Mr. Edmund Monson, and was sent to the Foreign Office on 20 April 1875.

According to the report, the wool clip for the season that had just ended was estimated at 68,000,000 pounds in weight, compared with 61,000,000 pounds the season before. The consul attributed this increase mainly to the spread of fencing across the estancias of the southern camps.

Of the total clip, about 26,000 bales were shipped to Havre, 19,000 bales went to Antwerp, and 11,500 bales were sent to Great Britain. Whatever remained was processed in local factories; the report noted that fourteen such factories were operating at the time, up from nine a year earlier.

The average price obtained at the sales was elevenpence per pound for greasy wool, which represented a decline of twopence farthing compared with the previous year. The consul also recorded that the S.A. Bienvenida sheep, first introduced by the Sociedad Rural in 1868, had by the most reliable estimates reached a total of 3,000,000 head, and that the wool from these sheep commanded a premium of one penny per pound above the ordinary criollo clip.

The report gave figures for transport and insurance costs: freight to London was quoted at five eighths of a penny per pound, while freight to Havre was a halfpenny farthing per pound; insurance on consignments to London ran at thirty-five shillings per cent.

Finally, the report closed with two observations about local improvements. The drainage of the flood-prone lands near Dolores, a project begun in 1873 under the direction of the engineer Mr. James Baine, had reclaimed approximately 400 square miles of pasture. In addition, the railway running from Tandil to the port, which had opened on 1 February of that year, had already succeeded in lowering cartage charges by two shillings per bale.

The text describes the surviving correspondence of Hagen and Sons, a Baltic timber firm, covering the month of March 1871. The exchange of letters begins with a communication dated 2 March from Christiania, sent by the firm's senior partner, Ludvig Hagen, to his brother Oscar, who was stationed at Riga. In this letter Ludvig directs Oscar to buy no more than 3,000 loads of pine deals, and not to pay more than 11 shillings per load, because news reaching them from Hull indicated that the market was falling. Oscar answered on 9 March, his reply travelling on the steamer Denmark. He reported that he had obtained 2,400 loads of first-quality Memel deals at 10 shillings and sixpence, and that he had turned down an additional 800 loads that had been offered at 12 shillings.

A letter of 17 March came from the firm's Hull agent, Whitfield and Company. It stated that over the previous fortnight 42 ships had arrived, compared with 29 in the corresponding period of the year before. The agent also reported that best Memel deals had dropped to 13 shillings and fourpence, representing a fall of ninepence. The same letter conveyed news of the failure of the house of Robertson and Maine, a firm that had held commitments in the timber trade amounting to 18,000 pounds, and it noted the expectation that this collapse would push prices down still further.

On 24 March, Ludvig Hagen wrote to the firm's bankers, the Discount Bank of Christiania, to arrange an overdraft of 6,000 pounds at an interest rate of five percent, the purpose being to cover drafts that would fall due in April. This same letter also recorded shipping information: the bark Alida had cleared Riga on 14 March carrying 1,100 deals consigned to Hull, with the cargo insured at Lloyd's for 2,750 pounds, and the steamer Denmark had been chartered for the return voyage at a rate of 45 pounds per day. **Record of the Royal Charter Commission Text**

The text describes an official inquiry into the wreck of the Royal Charter, a steam clipper ship. A commission was appointed to investigate the loss, and it held its sittings at Liverpool, beginning on 6 February 1860. The proceedings were conducted before Mr. Tremenheere, who was assisted by Captains Harris and Gray, both of the Board of Trade.

The vessel itself was of 2,719 tons register and had been built on the Clyde at Sandycroft in 1855. On her final voyage she departed Melbourne on 26 August 1859 carrying 388 passengers and a crew of 112. Her general cargo included 79,000 ounces of gold, packed in 39 boxes and consigned to banks in London. The ship was under the command of Captain John Taylor, who had sailed with her since her very first voyage.

The crossing to Britain took fifty-nine days and was made against heavy westerly winds. On the morning of 25 October, the ship rounded the Mull of Galloway and took two pilots aboard at Point Lynas. That same evening, the wind backed round to the northeast, and by ten o'clock it had increased to hurricane force. Although the ship's engines, rated at 200 nominal horsepower, were worked to their utmost, she drifted stern-first toward the coast of Anglesey. At half past one in the morning of 26 October, she struck the rocks half a mile east of Moelfre.

The account then details the rescue efforts. The first boat launched was stove in against the ship's side. A raft constructed by the carpenter, Peter Gibson, succeeded in carrying the purser and twenty men to shore, and a buoy line rigged by the mate, Joseph Rodgers, saved a further nineteen people. In total, 41 persons survived out of the 500 aboard. As for the gold, all but one of the consignments went down with the ship; a single box containing 1,640 ounces was recovered from the beach at Moelfre in November by a local man named Robert Williams.

Finally, the text sets out the commission's findings and recommendations. The commission concluded that the ship had been seaworthy and well found. It further found that the pilots had advised standing out to sea when the wind shifted, and that the decision to anchor in Moelfre roads had been taken by Captain Taylor against that advice. The commissioners recommended the establishment of a storm signal station at Point Lynas and a lifeboat at Moelfre, and both of these recommendations were carried out within two years by the Marine Board.

# Record of the Submarine Telegraph Company's Annual Report, 1868

The Submarine Telegraph Company produced its annual report covering the year that ended on 31 December 1868. This report was presented to the shareholders at a general meeting, which took place at the company's offices in Lothbury, London, on 11 February 1869. The meeting was chaired by the company's president, Sir Charles Bright.

The report set out the state of the company's operations. It disclosed that the company was then operating 1,940 nautical miles of submarine cable. Of this total, 310 miles had been laid during the year just ended, at a cost of 118,000 pounds. This new mileage consisted of two works: a new circuit running from Dover to Cape Grisnez, measuring 26 miles, and an extension from Cromer to Hanstholm, measuring 284 miles.

On the financial side, the report showed that the company's gross receipts for the year amounted to 147,300 pounds. This represented an increase of 11,200 pounds compared with the receipts of 1867. Within the total receipts, Continental messages accounted for 96,400 pounds, and these messages were charged at an average rate of four shillings and twopence each. The total number of messages transmitted during the year was 412,000, which worked out to a daily average of 1,127 messages.

The company's working expenses for the year were stated as 62,500 pounds. After deducting these expenses, the company was left with a net profit of 84,800 pounds. From this profit, the directors recommended that a dividend of seven percent be paid, which would absorb 59,000 pounds. The remaining 25,800 pounds was to be carried to the reserve fund, which, once this transfer was made, would stand at a total of 100,000 pounds.

The company's engineer, Mr. Latimer Clark, submitted his own report to the meeting. He stated that the failures experienced during the year had been limited to two faults in the Dover cable. The first of these faults occurred on 14 April and was caused by a ship's anchor at the Goodwins; it was repaired in nineteen hours. The second fault occurred on 3 August near the French shore; this one was repaired in two days, the work being carried out by the company's steamer, the Investigator, which was under the command of Captain Wood.

The report also gave figures for the company's workforce. As at the date of the report, the staff numbered 214 persons in total. Of these, 61 were clerks employed at the central station in Lothbury, and these clerks worked in three shifts of eight hours each.

The meeting came to a close with a vote of thanks to the chairman, which was carried unanimously.

# Record of the Submarine Telegraph Company's Annual Report, 1868

The Submarine Telegraph Company produced its annual report covering the year that ended on 31 December 1868. This report was presented to the shareholders at a general meeting, which took place at the company's offices in Lothbury, London, on 11 February 1869. The meeting was chaired by the company's president, Sir Charles Bright.
